concepts.title: Descriptive statistics
concepts.kw: descriptive statistics mean median mode standard deviation variance percentiles quartiles iqr range spread central tendency summary
concepts.s: Descriptive statistics summarise a column of numbers with a few values: where the centre is, how spread out it is, and what the extremes look like.
concepts.d: Centre is measured with the mean (the average), the median (the middle value) and the mode (the most common value). Spread is measured with the range, the standard deviation (the typical distance from the mean), and percentiles such as the 25th, 50th and 75th, whose gap is the interquartile range (IQR). When data is skewed, as order values and delivery times usually are, the median and percentiles describe a typical case better than the mean. Always report the count too, and look at a histogram before trusting any summary.
concepts.e: Delivery times in a city: mean 3.4 days, median 2 days, 90th percentile 7 days. The mean is pulled up by a few very late parcels, so "most orders arrive in 2 days, 1 in 10 takes a week or more" is the honest summary.
concepts.c: Average order value rose 10% but the median didn't move. What probably happened?
concepts.i: Expect when to use mean versus median, what standard deviation means, and how percentiles help describe service levels.

concepts.title: Distributions: normal, skewed and long-tailed
concepts.kw: distribution normal gaussian bell curve skewed right skew long tail power law log normal histogram heavy tail poisson
concepts.s: A distribution describes how often each value occurs. Recognising its shape tells you which summaries, tests and charts make sense.
concepts.d: A normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with about 68% of values within one standard deviation of the mean and 95% within two. Much business data is right-skewed instead: most values are small, with a long tail of large ones, as with order values, session lengths and customer spend. Long-tailed or power-law data means a few items dominate the total, such as top sellers or heavy users. Counts of events per period often follow a Poisson distribution. For skewed data, use medians and percentiles, log scales on charts, or a log transform before modelling.
concepts.e: Customer annual spend is right-skewed: the median customer spends Rs 2,400, but the top 5% spend over Rs 40,000 and account for 45% of revenue. A histogram on a log scale shows the shape clearly.
concepts.c: Why is the mean a poor summary of a long-tailed distribution?
concepts.i: Expect to describe common shapes, when the normal assumption fails, and how skew changes your choice of summary and chart.

concepts.title: Sampling and sampling bias
concepts.kw: sampling sample population random sample stratified sampling selection bias survivorship bias non response bias representative
concepts.s: A sample only tells you about a population if it represents it. Sampling bias happens when the way data was collected makes some groups more likely to appear than others.
concepts.d: A simple random sample gives every member the same chance of selection, and stratified sampling samples within groups, such as cities, to guarantee each is represented. Common biases: selection bias (only some users are included, like those who opted into a survey), survivorship bias (you only see those who stayed, like active customers), and non-response bias (people who answer differ from those who don't). A bigger biased sample doesn't fix bias; it just makes the wrong answer more precise. Always ask how the data was collected and who is missing.
concepts.e: A satisfaction survey sent to customers who placed a second order reports 92% satisfaction. It misses everyone who left after one bad experience, which is survivorship bias.
concepts.c: Why doesn't doubling the size of a biased sample fix the bias?
concepts.i: Interviewers give a scenario with a flawed sample and ask you to spot the bias and say how you'd collect data instead.

concepts.title: Confidence intervals
concepts.kw: confidence interval margin of error standard error uncertainty 95% interval estimate bootstrap precision sample size
concepts.s: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a quantity, such as a conversion rate, instead of a single number, showing how uncertain the estimate is.
concepts.d: A 95% confidence interval is built so that, if you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true value. For a mean or proportion it's roughly the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, and the standard error shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so four times the data halves the width. When formulas don't fit, the bootstrap resamples the data many times to estimate the interval. Reporting intervals stops people over-reading small differences between noisy numbers.
concepts.e: Checkout conversion is 4.0% from 2,500 sessions. The standard error is about 0.39 points, so the 95% interval is roughly 3.2% to 4.8%. Last week's 4.3% is inside it, so the "drop" may just be noise.
concepts.c: How much more data do you need to halve the width of a confidence interval?
concepts.i: Expect to interpret an interval correctly, explain the effect of sample size, and use intervals when comparing two groups.

concepts.title: Hypothesis testing and p-values
concepts.kw: hypothesis testing null hypothesis alternative p-value significance level alpha type i error type ii error t-test chi-square z-test
concepts.s: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is larger than you'd expect from random chance alone.
concepts.d: You start with a null hypothesis, usually "no difference", and compute a p-value: the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the null were true. If it's below the significance level alpha, often 0.05, you reject the null. A type I error is a false positive (rejecting a true null) and a type II error is a false negative (missing a real effect). Common tests: a t-test for means, a z-test or chi-square test for proportions and counts. A p-value isn't the probability that the hypothesis is true, and a significant result can still be too small to matter.
concepts.e: Variant B converts at 5.2% against 4.8% for control, over 20,000 users each. A two-proportion z-test gives p = 0.06, so at alpha 0.05 you can't conclude B is better yet.
concepts.c: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually tell you?
concepts.i: Expect the definitions of p-value, alpha and the two error types, and which test fits a given metric.

concepts.title: Correlation vs causation
concepts.kw: correlation causation confounder confounding variable spurious correlation reverse causality simpson's paradox pearson randomised experiment
concepts.s: Two metrics moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. A hidden third factor, chance, or causation in the other direction can explain it.
concepts.d: Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together, from -1 to 1, and Pearson's coefficient only captures linear relationships. A confounder affects both variables, such as seasonality driving both ad spend and sales. Reverse causality means the effect actually drives the cause. Simpson's paradox is when a trend in every group reverses once groups are combined, because group sizes differ. To claim causation you need a randomised experiment, or careful quasi-experimental methods when you can't randomise.
concepts.e: Cities with more delivery partners have more late deliveries. Partners don't cause lateness; bigger, busier cities have both more partners and more traffic, which is a confounder.
concepts.c: Customers who use the app's wishlist spend 40% more. Why can't you say the wishlist makes them spend more?
concepts.i: Interviewers test this with a scenario and ask how you'd find out whether the relationship is causal.

concepts.title: Detecting and handling outliers
concepts.kw: outliers outlier detection iqr rule z-score winsorise winsorize cap trim anomaly extreme values robust statistics median
concepts.s: Outliers are values far from the rest. Some are errors to fix, and some are real and important, so you investigate before removing anything.
concepts.d: Detect them visually with box plots and histograms, or with rules such as values beyond 1.5 times the IQR from the quartiles, or a z-score above 3 for roughly normal data. Then find the cause: data entry or unit errors (an amount in paise instead of rupees), test or bot traffic, or genuine extremes such as a bulk B2B order. Fix errors, exclude test traffic with a documented rule, and keep genuine values but use robust summaries like the median, or cap (winsorise) them for specific analyses. Always report what you removed and why.
concepts.e: One order of Rs 9,99,999 triples the day's average order value. It turns out to be an internal test order, so it's excluded by a rule filtering test accounts, and the rule is documented.
concepts.c: Why shouldn't you delete every value with a z-score above 3?
concepts.i: Expect how you'd detect outliers, how you'd decide whether to keep them, and how they affect means and models.

concepts.title: Funnel analysis
concepts.kw: funnel analysis conversion steps drop off step conversion rate checkout funnel visit product cart payment order abandonment
concepts.s: Funnel analysis measures how many users move through each step of a journey, such as visit, product view, add to cart, checkout and payment, and where they drop off.
concepts.d: Define the steps and the order they must happen in, the counting unit (users or sessions) and the time window for completing the funnel. Step conversion is the share reaching step n+1 out of those at step n, and overall conversion is the last step over the first. The biggest absolute drop shows where to focus, and breaking the funnel down by device, channel, city or new versus returning users shows where it's broken. In SQL, compute each user's first time at each step and count users whose steps happen in order within the window.
concepts.e: Of 100,000 visitors, 40,000 view a product, 8,000 add to cart, 3,000 start checkout and 2,100 pay. The cart-to-checkout step loses 62%, and on Android it loses 75%, pointing to an app bug.
concepts.c: Why should a funnel count users who did the steps in order within a time window, rather than just counting each event?
concepts.i: Analyst interviews ask you to define a funnel, write the SQL for it, and explain how you'd investigate a drop at one step.

concepts.title: Retention and churn metrics
concepts.kw: retention churn rate active users dau mau stickiness repeat purchase rolling retention n-day retention customer lifetime cohort
concepts.s: Retention measures how many customers keep coming back, and churn measures how many stop. Both need a precise definition of "active".
concepts.d: N-day retention is the share of a cohort active on day N after their start; rolling retention counts them if active on day N or later. For subscriptions, churn is the share of subscribers who cancel in a period. For non-subscription businesses, churn has to be defined with an inactivity window, such as no order in 90 days. DAU/MAU measures stickiness. Always measure retention by cohort, because a growing user base can hide worsening retention, and choose the activity that reflects real value, such as an order rather than an app open.
concepts.e: Month-1 repeat purchase rate fell from 32% for January's cohort to 24% for April's, even though total monthly buyers grew, because heavy discounting brought in deal-seekers who didn't return.
concepts.c: Why define churn for a grocery app as "no order in 60 days" rather than "uninstalled the app"?
concepts.i: Expect to define retention and churn for a given product, write the cohort SQL, and suggest what drives changes.

concepts.title: Unit economics: CAC, LTV, AOV and margin
concepts.kw: unit economics cac customer acquisition cost ltv clv lifetime value aov average order value contribution margin payback period ratio
concepts.s: Unit economics asks whether each customer or order makes money once all its direct costs are included.
concepts.d: Average order value (AOV) is revenue divided by orders. Contribution margin per order is revenue minus variable costs such as product cost, delivery, payment fees, discounts and returns. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is marketing and sales spend divided by new customers acquired. Lifetime value (LTV) is the contribution margin a customer generates over their life, roughly margin per order times orders per year times expected lifetime. A healthy business has LTV well above CAC, often three times or more, and a short payback period. Calculate them by channel and cohort, not just overall.
concepts.e: Instagram ads bring customers at a CAC of Rs 600. They place 4 orders a year with Rs 120 contribution margin each, for an expected 2 years, so LTV is about Rs 960 and the LTV to CAC ratio is only 1.6.
concepts.c: Why should LTV use contribution margin rather than revenue?
concepts.i: Expect to calculate CAC, LTV and contribution margin from numbers, and to judge whether a channel or promotion is worth it.

concepts.title: Root-cause analysis of metric changes
concepts.kw: root cause analysis metric drop investigate decline segment breakdown mix shift seasonality tracking bug data issue diagnose why did revenue fall
concepts.s: When a key metric suddenly changes, a structured investigation separates data problems from real changes and finds which segment and cause explain it.
concepts.d: First confirm the change is real: check data freshness, tracking or pipeline changes, and definition changes. Then put it in context against seasonality, the same day last week and last year, and holidays or events. Decompose the metric into its parts, for example revenue equals sessions times conversion times AOV, to see which part moved. Slice by segments such as platform, city, channel, new versus returning, and product category to find where the change is concentrated, and watch for mix shift, where totals change because the mix of segments changes. Finally, connect it to internal changes (releases, prices, campaigns) and external ones (competitors, outages, weather).
concepts.e: Orders fell 12% on Tuesday. Sessions were flat and conversion fell only on iOS, starting just after the 6.2 app release, which had broken the saved-address screen.
concepts.c: Revenue is down 8%. What's the first thing you check before slicing by segment?
concepts.i: This is a classic analytics case question: explain your step-by-step approach to diagnosing a metric drop.

concepts.title: Customer segmentation and RFM
concepts.kw: segmentation customer segments rfm recency frequency monetary clustering personas champions at risk targeting quintiles
concepts.s: Segmentation groups customers who behave similarly, so marketing, product and service can treat them differently. RFM is a simple, effective method based on purchase behaviour.
concepts.d: RFM scores each customer on recency (days since the last order), frequency (number of orders) and monetary value (total spend), usually as quintiles from 1 to 5. Combinations form named segments: champions buy recently, often and a lot; at-risk customers used to buy often but haven't recently; new customers have high recency but low frequency. Rule-based segments are easy to explain and act on, while clustering such as k-means can find less obvious groups. Good segments are measurable, large enough to matter, and lead to different actions.
concepts.e: Champions (R5, F5) get early access to sales, while at-risk customers (R1-2, F4-5) get a win-back offer. The win-back campaign recovers 11% of them within a month.
concepts.c: Why score RFM with quintiles rather than fixed thresholds like "more than 5 orders"?
concepts.i: Expect to explain RFM, write the SQL for it, and say what actions you'd take for each segment.

concepts.title: Statistical power and sample size
concepts.kw: statistical power sample size minimum detectable effect mde power analysis type ii error baseline conversion alpha beta 80% duration
concepts.s: Power is the chance an experiment detects a real effect of a given size. A power analysis tells you how many users you need before you start.
concepts.d: Sample size depends on four things: the baseline rate or variance of the metric, the minimum detectable effect (MDE) you care about, the significance level (often 5%), and the power (often 80%). Smaller effects and noisier metrics need much more data: halving the MDE needs about four times the sample. An underpowered test will usually come back flat even when the change works, and the significant results it does find tend to overestimate the effect. Convert the sample size into a duration using daily traffic, and run whole weeks to cover weekly patterns.
concepts.e: Baseline conversion is 4% and you want to detect a lift to 4.4% (a 10% relative MDE) with 80% power at alpha 0.05. That needs about 39,000 users per group, so with 10,000 eligible users a day the test runs for 8 days, rounded up to two full weeks.
concepts.c: Why does halving the minimum detectable effect roughly quadruple the sample size?
concepts.i: Expect to explain power, MDE and what drives sample size, and what you'd do if traffic is too low.

concepts.title: Peeking and multiple testing
concepts.kw: peeking early stopping multiple testing multiple comparisons false positives bonferroni false discovery rate sequential testing many metrics variants
concepts.s: Checking results repeatedly or testing many metrics and variants greatly increases the chance of a false positive, unless you correct for it.
concepts.d: With alpha at 5%, each test has a 1 in 20 chance of a false positive. Peeking at a running test every day and stopping when it's significant can push the real false positive rate to 20% or more. Testing 20 metrics or many variants means one will probably look significant by chance. Fixes: decide the sample size and duration up front and analyse once, use sequential testing methods designed for continuous monitoring, pick one primary metric in advance, and adjust for multiple comparisons with Bonferroni or false discovery rate control. Treat surprising wins in secondary metrics as ideas for new tests.
concepts.e: A team checked a test daily and stopped on day 4 when p was 0.03. A rerun for the planned two weeks showed no effect: the early result was noise caught by peeking.
concepts.c: You tested 15 metrics and one is significant at p = 0.04. How confident should you be?
concepts.i: Senior analyst and data science interviews ask why peeking is a problem and how you'd control false positives across metrics.

concepts.title: Quasi-experiments and difference-in-differences
concepts.kw: quasi experiment difference in differences did parallel trends synthetic control regression discontinuity natural experiment causal inference observational
concepts.s: When you can't run a randomised test, quasi-experimental methods estimate causal effects from observational data, under assumptions you must check.
concepts.d: Difference-in-differences compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in a similar untreated group, so shared trends like seasonality cancel out. Its key assumption is parallel trends: without the change, both groups would have moved alike, which you check by comparing their trends before the change. Synthetic control builds a weighted mix of untreated units that matches the treated unit before the change. Regression discontinuity compares units just above and below a cut-off. Natural experiments use events that assign treatment almost randomly. All of them rely on assumptions, so state them and test them where possible.
concepts.e: Free delivery launched in Pune but not in Nagpur. Pune's orders rose 18% and Nagpur's 6% over the same period, so the difference-in-differences estimate is about 12 points, after checking both cities trended alike for the six months before.
concepts.c: What's the parallel trends assumption, and how do you check it?
concepts.i: Expect when you'd use these methods instead of an A/B test, how difference-in-differences works, and its assumptions.

questions.q: When would you report the median instead of the mean?

p.t: Median when the data is skewed
Outliers pull the mean
Median represents a typical case
Example such as order value or delivery time
Report percentiles too

questions.a: When the data is skewed or has outliers, because a few extreme values pull the mean up while the median, the middle value, stays put and better represents a typical case. Order value, delivery time and income are usually right-skewed, so I'd report the median and percentiles such as the 90th, for example most orders arrive in 2 days and 1 in 10 takes over a week.

questions.q: Average order value went up 10%, but the median didn't change. What could explain it?

p.t: A few large orders raised the mean
The median is robust to the tail
Check for outliers or test or B2B orders
Look at the distribution or percentiles

questions.a: Most likely a few very large orders raised the mean while typical orders were unchanged, since the median is robust to what happens in the tail. I'd check for outliers, such as bulk B2B orders, a test order or a pricing error, and look at the distribution with a histogram and the 90th and 99th percentiles to see whether the top end moved.

questions.q: What does it mean that a metric is right-skewed, and how does that change your analysis?

p.t: Most values small, long tail of large values
Mean above the median
Use median or percentiles
Log scale or log transform
A few items dominate the total

questions.a: Most values are small, with a long tail of large values, like customer spend or session length. The mean is above the median because the tail pulls it up, so I'd summarise with the median and percentiles. For charts I'd use a log scale, and for modelling often a log transform. It also means a few customers or products dominate the total, which is worth showing separately.

questions.q: When is assuming a normal distribution reasonable, and when does it fail?

p.t: Symmetric data without heavy tails
Averages of large samples (central limit theorem)
Fails for skewed or heavy-tailed data
Fails for bounded counts or rates
Check with a histogram or Q-Q plot

questions.a: It's reasonable for symmetric data without heavy tails, like measurement errors, and for averages of large samples, because the central limit theorem makes sample means roughly normal even when the data isn't. It fails for skewed or heavy-tailed data like revenue per customer, and for small counts or bounded rates, where a Poisson or binomial model fits better. I'd check with a histogram or a Q-Q plot before relying on it.

questions.q: A satisfaction survey was sent only to customers who placed a second order. What's wrong with the result?

p.t: Not representative of all customers
Survivorship bias: unhappy customers left
Non-response bias as well
Sample a random or stratified set of all customers

questions.a: The sample isn't representative of all customers. It suffers from survivorship bias, because customers who left after a bad first order never received it, so satisfaction will look too high. There's also non-response bias, since people who answer surveys differ from those who don't. I'd survey a random sample of all customers, or a stratified sample across first-time and repeat buyers, and compare response rates.

questions.q: Name three kinds of sampling bias and give an example of each.

p.t: Selection bias
Survivorship bias
Non-response bias
More data doesn't fix bias

questions.a: Selection bias: only users who opted in to a beta are studied, and they're more engaged than average. Survivorship bias: analysing only active customers hides why others churned. Non-response bias: people who don't reply to a survey differ from those who do, for example busy, less satisfied users. In each case a bigger sample doesn't help; more data just makes the biased answer more precise.

questions.q: How would you explain a 95% confidence interval to a product manager?

p.t: A range of plausible values
Reflects uncertainty from sampling
95% of such intervals would contain the true value
Wider with less data
Overlapping ranges mean differences may be noise

questions.a: It's a range of plausible values for the true number, reflecting how uncertain our estimate is from sampling. If we repeated the measurement many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true value. Less data gives a wider interval. So if conversion is 4.0% with an interval of 3.2% to 4.8%, a reading of 4.3% last week could easily be noise, and we shouldn't react to it.

questions.q: How does sample size affect the width of a confidence interval?

p.t: Standard error falls with the square root of n
Four times the data halves the width
Diminishing returns
Variance of the metric matters too

questions.a: The width is driven by the standard error, which falls with the square root of the sample size. So four times the data halves the width, and you get diminishing returns from adding more. The metric's variance matters too: noisier metrics, like revenue per user, need far more data for the same precision than a conversion rate.

questions.q: What is a p-value, and what is it not?

p.t: Probability of a result this extreme if the null is true
Compared with alpha
Not the probability the hypothesis is true
Doesn't measure effect size

questions.a: A p-value is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis, usually no difference, were true. If it's below alpha, often 0.05, we reject the null. It isn't the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the result is due to chance. And it doesn't measure effect size: a tiny, unimportant difference can be significant with enough data, so I always report how big the effect is too.

questions.q: Explain type I and type II errors with a business example.

p.t: Type I is a false positive
Type II is a false negative
Alpha controls type I
Power controls type II
Business example of the cost

questions.a: A type I error is a false positive: we conclude a new checkout design works when it doesn't, and ship a change with no benefit. A type II error is a false negative: the design really works but the test misses it, so we lose a real improvement. The significance level alpha controls the type I rate, and power, driven mainly by sample size, controls the type II rate. Which matters more depends on the cost of each mistake.

questions.q: Wishlist users spend 40% more. Can you say the wishlist increases spending?

p.t: Correlation, not causation
Selection or confounding: engaged users use it
Reverse causality
Run a randomised experiment

questions.a: No, that's a correlation, not causation. The likely confounder is engagement: customers who already shop a lot are the ones who use the wishlist, which is also selection. There could be reverse causality too: people planning big purchases create wishlists. To measure the real effect I'd run a randomised experiment, for example promoting the wishlist to a random half of users and comparing their spend.

questions.q: What is Simpson's paradox? Give an example.

p.t: A trend in every group reverses when combined
Caused by different group sizes or mix
A concrete example
Always check the segment breakdown

questions.a: Simpson's paradox is when a trend that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined, because the group sizes or mix differ. For example, a new courier partner has a better on-time rate than the old one in every city, yet worse overall, because it handles mostly the difficult metro city, where everyone is late more often. So I always check the segment breakdown before trusting a combined comparison.

questions.q: How do you detect outliers, and how do you decide what to do with them?

p.t: Box plots, histograms, IQR or z-score rules
Investigate the cause first
Fix errors and exclude test data
Keep real extremes but use robust measures or capping
Document what was removed

questions.a: Detect them with box plots and histograms, or rules such as beyond 1.5 times the IQR from the quartiles, or a z-score above 3. Then investigate the cause before removing anything. Errors such as wrong units get fixed, and test or bot traffic gets excluded with a clear rule. Genuine extremes, like a bulk order, stay in, but I use robust measures such as the median, or cap them (winsorise) for specific analyses. I document what was removed and why.

questions.q: How do outliers affect means and models, and how can you reduce their influence?

p.t: They pull the mean and standard deviation
They distort linear models and squared-error losses
Use robust statistics or losses
Transform or cap values
Tree models are less sensitive

questions.a: A single extreme value can pull the mean and inflate the standard deviation. In models, linear regression with squared-error loss gives extreme points a lot of weight and can tilt the whole fit. To reduce their influence I'd use robust statistics like the median or robust losses such as Huber, apply a log transform or cap values at a percentile, or use tree models, which are less sensitive because they split on order rather than magnitude.

questions.q: How would you build a checkout funnel in SQL?

p.t: Define the steps and the counting unit
First time each user reached each step
Steps in order within a time window
Count users per step and step conversion
Break down by segment

questions.a: First define the steps (product view, add to cart, checkout, payment) and count users, not events. For each user, find the first time they reached each step with MIN(event_time) grouped by user and step, pivoted into columns with CASE. A user counts at a step only if they reached it after the previous step and within a time window, for example within one day of the first step. Then count users per step and divide each by the previous step for step conversion. Finally break it down by device and channel to find where it's broken.

questions.q: The add-to-cart to checkout step dropped from 45% to 35% this week. How do you investigate?

p.t: Check tracking and data issues first
Segment by platform, browser and app version
Look for releases or changes
Check external factors and mix
Confirm with session data or replays

questions.a: First rule out a tracking or data issue, such as a renamed checkout event or a delayed pipeline. Then segment by platform, browser, app version, city and new versus returning users to see where the drop is concentrated. Compare the timing with releases, price or delivery-fee changes and payment outages. Also check traffic mix: a campaign bringing low-intent users can lower the rate without anything breaking. Finally confirm with session data or replays of users who dropped.

questions.q: How would you define churn for a grocery delivery app?

p.t: No subscription, so use an inactivity window
Base the window on purchase intervals
Activity means an order, not an app open
Measure by cohort
Validate the definition

questions.a: There's no subscription to cancel, so churn needs an inactivity window, for example no order in 60 days. I'd base the window on the typical purchase interval or time between orders: if 90% of repeat orders come within 45 days, 60 days is a sensible cut-off. Activity should mean an order, not an app open, because orders reflect real value. I'd measure churn by cohort, and validate the definition by checking how few churned customers come back later.

questions.q: Total active users are growing, but leadership worries about retention. How would you analyse it?

p.t: Cohort retention curves
Growth can hide worse retention
Compare cohorts at the same age
Segment by acquisition channel or promotion
Link to drivers like first-order experience

questions.a: I'd build cohort retention curves by signup month, because growth from new users can hide worsening retention in the total. Comparing cohorts at the same age, such as month 1 and month 3 repeat rates, shows whether newer cohorts retain worse. Then segment by acquisition channel and promotion, since heavy discounts often bring deal-seekers who don't return. Finally link retention to drivers like the first-order experience: late deliveries or missing items on the first order.

questions.q: How do you calculate CAC and LTV, and how do you use them together?

p.t: CAC is acquisition spend over new customers
LTV uses contribution margin over the lifetime
Orders per year and expected lifetime
Compare LTV to CAC and payback
Calculate by channel and cohort

questions.a: CAC is marketing and sales spend divided by the number of new customers acquired in the period. LTV is the contribution margin a customer generates over their life: margin per order times orders per year times expected lifetime in years, ideally from real cohort data. I compare them as an LTV to CAC ratio, wanting it around three or more, and look at the payback period. They must be calculated by channel and cohort, because averages hide unprofitable channels.

questions.q: A promotion raised orders 30%. How would you judge whether it was worth it?

p.t: Incremental orders vs a baseline or control
Contribution margin after the discount
Pull-forward and cannibalisation
Retention of customers acquired
Compare total profit

questions.a: A 30% rise in orders isn't the answer by itself. First estimate incremental orders against a baseline or control group, since some would have happened anyway. Then compute contribution margin after the discount, delivery and payment costs. Check for pull-forward, where customers just bought earlier, and cannibalisation of full-price sales. Look at whether customers acquired through the promotion come back. The promotion was worth it only if net profit over that period, including those effects, beats doing nothing.

questions.q: Daily orders dropped 12% yesterday. Walk me through your investigation.

p.t: Confirm the data is right
Compare with seasonality and the same day last week
Decompose the metric
Slice by segment to find where it's concentrated
Link to internal and external events

questions.a: First confirm the drop is real: check the pipeline loaded fully, tracking didn't change, and the definition is the same. Then put it in context with seasonality, comparing with the same day last week and last year, and holidays. Next decompose orders into sessions times conversion to see which part moved. Then slice by segment, such as platform, city, channel and new versus returning, to find where the drop is concentrated. Finally match the timing to internal events like a release or price change, and external ones like a payment outage or a competitor sale.

questions.q: What is a mix shift, and how can it mislead a metric investigation?

p.t: The total changes because the segment mix changes
Each segment can be flat or improving
A concrete example
Separate rate and mix effects

questions.a: A mix shift is when an overall metric changes because the mix of segments changes, not because any segment changed. Each segment's rate can be flat or even improving while the total falls. For example, overall conversion drops because a campaign brought many new users, who always convert less, even though conversion for new and returning users both held steady. To avoid being misled I separate the rate effect within segments from the mix effect of changing segment sizes.

questions.q: How would you build an RFM segmentation in SQL?

p.t: Compute recency, frequency and monetary per customer
Score with quintiles using NTILE
Combine scores into named segments
Choose a time window
Actions per segment

questions.a: For each customer over a time window, say the last 12 months, compute recency as days since the last order, frequency as the number of orders, and monetary as total spend, with a GROUP BY on customer. Score each with quintiles using NTILE(5) over the ordered values, reversing recency so recent customers score 5. Then combine scores into named segments with CASE, such as champions for high recency and frequency, and at risk for high frequency but low recency. Each segment gets its own action, like a win-back offer for at-risk customers.

questions.q: When would you use rule-based segments like RFM versus clustering?

p.t: Rules are simple and explainable
Rules map directly to actions
Clustering finds less obvious groups
Clusters need scaling and interpretation
Segments must be stable and large enough

questions.a: Rule-based segments like RFM are simple, easy to explain to marketing, and map directly to actions such as a campaign for at-risk customers. Clustering, such as k-means on many behavioural features, can find less obvious groups, like weekend bulk buyers, but needs feature scaling, choosing the number of clusters, and work to interpret and name each cluster. Either way, segments must be stable over time and large enough to act on.

questions.q: What determines the sample size an A/B test needs?

p.t: Baseline rate or variance
Minimum detectable effect
Significance level
Power, usually 80%
Convert to duration with full weeks

questions.a: Four things: the baseline rate or variance of the metric, the minimum detectable effect (MDE) you care about, the significance level alpha, usually 5%, and the power, usually 80%. Smaller effects and noisier metrics need much larger samples; halving the MDE needs about four times the users. Then convert the sample size into a duration using daily traffic, and run full weeks to cover weekday patterns.

questions.q: Your product only gets 2,000 users a week, too few for a well-powered test. What can you do?

p.t: Accept a larger MDE or run longer
Use a more sensitive or higher-rate metric
Reduce variance with CUPED or covariates
Test bolder changes
Use qualitative or quasi-experimental evidence

questions.a: Options: accept a larger MDE or run longer, only testing for a bigger effect. Use a more sensitive metric, such as add-to-cart rate instead of purchases, which has a higher rate and needs fewer users. Reduce variance with CUPED, which adjusts for each user's pre-experiment behaviour. Test bolder changes that could plausibly have big effects. And where a test isn't practical, combine qualitative research with quasi-experimental methods.

questions.q: Why is it a problem to check an A/B test every day and stop as soon as it's significant?

p.t: Each look is another chance of a false positive
The real error rate rises well above 5%
Results fluctuate early
Fix the sample size up front
Or use sequential testing

questions.a: Each look is another chance for random noise to cross the significance line, so stopping at the first significant result raises the false positive rate well above 5%, often to 20% or more with daily checks. Early results fluctuate a lot and tend to exaggerate effects. The fix is to fix the sample size and duration up front and analyse once at the end, or, if you need to monitor continuously, use sequential testing methods designed for it.

questions.q: You tested 15 metrics and 1 came out significant at p = 0.04. What do you conclude?

p.t: Expected by chance with many metrics
Multiple comparisons problem
Corrections: Bonferroni or false discovery rate
Pre-register a primary metric
Treat it as a hypothesis to retest

questions.a: Very little. With 15 metrics at alpha 0.05, getting one significant result is close to what you'd expect by chance, which is the multiple comparisons problem. After a Bonferroni correction, the threshold would be about 0.0033, or with false discovery rate control it would also likely not survive. That's why the primary metric should be chosen in advance. I'd treat this result as a hypothesis and confirm it with a new test.

questions.q: Free delivery launched in one city but not others. How would you measure its effect without an A/B test?

p.t: Difference-in-differences with a comparison city
Before and after in both groups
Check parallel pre-trends
Synthetic control as an alternative
Watch for other changes at the same time

questions.a: I'd use difference-in-differences: pick a comparison city, or several, that didn't get free delivery, and compare the change over time in orders before and after the launch in both groups. The effect is the treated city's change minus the comparison city's change, so shared trends like seasonality cancel out. It relies on parallel trends, so I'd check both cities moved alike for months before the launch. Synthetic control is an alternative, building a weighted mix of cities that matches the treated one. I'd also check for other changes at the same time, such as a marketing campaign, which would confound the result.

questions.q: When would you use a quasi-experiment instead of an A/B test, and what are the risks?

p.t: Randomisation impossible, unethical or too costly
Examples like pricing, city launches or past events
Methods such as DiD, regression discontinuity or synthetic control
Rely on untestable assumptions
Hidden confounders can bias the result

questions.a: When you can't randomise, because it's unethical, too costly, or the change applies to a whole market, such as a city launch, a pricing change, or an event that already happened. Methods include difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and synthetic control. The risk is that they rely on assumptions that can't be fully tested, like parallel trends, so hidden confounders can bias the result. I'd state the assumptions, run robustness checks, and present the result with that caveat.
